conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply 10 questions about the past seven days; it isn’t a test, and there are no right or wrong answers. Everything you share stays confidential, and our only goal is to make sure you feel supported and safe. Ready to start?  

First question: Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy the little things that used to make you smile, or has that enjoyment slipped away?

Honestly? Most of the things that used to feel fun—like scrolling through silly videos or grabbing coffee with a friend—just feel kind of… flat. I try to watch a show while I nurse, but I barely laugh. It’s like the color’s been drained out. I still get little sparks, like when the baby gives me that milk-drunk smile, but even that warm feeling fades fast and I’m back to feeling blah.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute meme, but it’s over in a second. Real laughter feels out of reach. My partner tried to joke about the diaper explosions and I just couldn’t find it funny; I mostly felt tired and a little annoyed.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much. I used to get excited about little outings—like even just a walk to the coffee shop—but now when I think about doing anything, it feels like one more chore. I tell myself, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like it,” but tomorrow comes and I still don’t really care.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I missed his sleepy cues.” Yesterday he spit up a ton after a feeding and I kept replaying it, convinced I’d over-fed him or eaten something bad. My partner says it’s normal baby stuff, but I can’t shake the feeling that I messed up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep in the bassinet and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too quiet—so I jump up to check if he’s breathing. Even when nothing’s happening, there’s this constant buzz in my chest like something bad is about to go wrong. I know it sounds silly, but I can’t switch it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and for a minute I’m convinced something horrible is about to happen even though the room is calm and the baby’s fine. Last night I had to put him in the crib, pace the hallway, and do those breathing exercises the nurse showed us just to get my heart to slow down.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some days it feels like I’m drowning in little tasks. The dishes pile up, the laundry buzzer goes off, the baby wants to cluster-feed, and I just stand there wondering how I’ll get through the next hour. I usually manage to keep us both fed and safe, but it’s like I’m barely treading water and I’m exhausted the whole time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s me most nights. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed myself, and then my head starts spinning—did I sterilize the pump parts, is he gaining enough weight, am I already failing him? It takes forever to drift off, and if he so much as squeaks I’m wide awake again. I’m lucky if I get three or four broken hours before morning.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty often. I’ll just be rocking the baby and tears start coming. I feel heavy and flat, like I’m wearing a lead blanket. Sometimes I look at other moms on social media who seem so happy and connected, and I think, “Why can’t I feel like that?” I hate that I’m missing these sweet newborn weeks because I’m stuck in this fog.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... it’s happened three, maybe four times this week. Little things set me off—like running out of diapers and realizing I have to drag us to the store, or looking in the mirror and not recognizing my body. The tears just come and I can’t stop them right away. It’s not sobbing all day, but it keeps catching me off guard.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… never. When I feel really low, I do get scared that I’m not doing a good job, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby needs.

You've shared how the joy and color seem to have drained from daily life since your baby arrived: humor feels distant, simple outings now loom like chores, and waves of <sym>anxiety</sym> and self-blame crash over you many times a day. Yet through the <sym>tearfulness</sym>, <sym>exhaustion</sym>, and nights of broken <sym>sleep</sym>, you remain devoted to your baby and determined to feel better so you can savor these early weeks.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of ability to laugh; momentary smiles fade instantly and all humor feels inaccessible.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses blaming herself "a lot" and provides multiple examples of self-blame for routine infant behavior, indicating this happens most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, physiologic anxiety with catastrophic thoughts and persistent bodily tension, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of intense panic with physical symptoms, occurring "a few times"—clearly fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks and exhaustion, indicating she is "barely treading water"—matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent sadness with crying spells, anhedonia, and comparison distress—closely aligns with "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by minor stressors, indicating frequent though not constant tearfulness, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 23 (≥14) places you in the high-risk category. Qualitative responses map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: nearly constant low mood and loss of interest <quote>the color's been drained out</quote>, multiple daily crying spells, inappropriate guilt <quote>I must be doing something wrong</quote>, fatigue, impaired concentration, and anxiety with recurrent panic symptoms. Item 10 score of 0 indicates no current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and consider <med>sertraline</med> or other <med>SSRI</med> if clinically indicated
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress
4. Plan daily 15-minute mood check-ins with your partner; keep a simple log of sleep, appetite, and crying spells
5. Prioritize rest: accept help for night feeds, nap when baby naps, limit visitors, and practice 4-7-8 breathing for <sym>panic</sym> surges
6. Connect with local <med>postpartum support group</med> or online communities to reduce isolation
7. If any thoughts of self-harm develop, contact your provider immediately or call a crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Mother via self-report (10-item EPDS-style questionnaire)

Symptoms & Observations  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Daily, distressing anxiety and panic episodes without clear trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “drowning” in routine tasks (Q6)  
- Sleep disruption driven by intrusive worries after infant is settled (Q7)  

Pattern: Symptoms present most days for ≥2 weeks, interfere with ADLs and parenting confidence; no enjoyment in previously pleasurable activities.

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10). No current protective concerns for infant.

Screening Significance: Score pattern and qualitative responses indicate elevated risk for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety. Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR criteria) and discussion of support / treatment options.
